options.text: No row at all, because Cy has no matching order
options.why: That is inner-join behaviour. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table.

options.text: One row: Cy with NULL in every order column
options.why: Unmatched left rows are kept once and padded with NULLs for the right table.

options.text: One row: Cy paired with order 13, the order with no customer
options.why: Order 13 has a NULL customer_id, which never equals 3, so it is not paired with Cy.

options.text: Four rows: Cy paired with each order in turn
options.why: Pairing with every order is what a CROSS JOIN does; the ON condition still applies here.

explanation: A LEFT JOIN returns all inner-join rows, plus each left row with no match, extended with NULLs for the right-hand columns. Cy has no orders, so the result has `(Cy, NULL, NULL)`. The query returns 4 rows in total.

`orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id` returns the same rows as `customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`.

options.text: True
options.why: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table, so swapping the table order turns it into the equivalent LEFT JOIN.

options.text: False
options.why: Both keep all customers and pad unmatched ones with NULLs; only the column order in SELECT * would differ.

explanation: `A RIGHT JOIN B` is defined as `B LEFT JOIN A`. Both queries return Ann twice, Bob once, and Cy once with NULL order columns: 4 rows. Most teams write only LEFT JOINs because they read left to right more easily.

stem: Match each join type with the rows it returns.

options.text: Only pairs of rows where the join condition is true
Every row of the left table, plus matching right rows or NULLs
Every row from both tables, matched where possible and NULL-padded otherwise
Every combination of a left row with a right row

explanation: Inner joins keep matching pairs only. Outer joins add the unmatched rows from one side (LEFT or RIGHT) or both (FULL), padding the missing side with NULLs. A CROSS JOIN has no condition and returns the Cartesian product.

stem: A `colors` table has 3 rows and a `sizes` table has 4 rows. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM colors CROSS JOIN sizes;` return? Type a number.
explanation: A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of the other: 3 × 4 = 12. It is useful for generating combinations (every colour in every size), and dangerous when it happens by accident.

stem: `staff(id, name, manager_id)` holds `(1, 'Ceo', NULL)`, `(2, 'Vp', 1)` and `(3, 'Dev', 2)`. Which query lists every employee with their manager's name, including the CEO?

options.text: `FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id`
options.why: An inner join drops the CEO, whose manager_id is NULL and so matches no row.

options.text: `FROM staff e LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id`
options.why: Each employee row looks up its manager; the CEO is kept with a NULL manager name.

options.text: `FROM staff e LEFT JOIN staff m ON e.id = m.manager_id`
options.why: This pairs each person with their direct reports, not with their manager.

options.text: `FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.manager_id = e.manager_id`
options.why: This pairs colleagues who share a manager, and still drops the CEO.

explanation: A self join treats one table as two roles. Alias `e` is the employee and `m` the manager, matched by `m.id = e.manager_id`. LEFT JOIN keeps the employee whose manager is missing. Result: (Ceo, NULL), (Vp, Ceo), (Dev, Vp).

Order 13 never appears in `customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`. Why?

options.text: Joins skip any row that has a NULL in any of its columns
options.why: Only the join condition matters; NULLs in other columns are carried through normally.

options.text: Comparing NULL with any id gives NULL, never true, so the row matches nothing
options.why: Join conditions use three-valued logic; only rows where the condition is true are joined.

options.text: PostgreSQL removes rows with NULL keys from the right-hand table before running any join
options.why: No such pre-filtering happens; the row simply never satisfies the condition.

options.text: Inner joins keep only orders whose amount exceeds the smallest order
options.why: The amount plays no part here; only `o.customer_id = c.id` decides matches.

explanation: `NULL = 1` evaluates to NULL (unknown), and a join keeps a pair only when its condition is true. So a NULL foreign key matches no row, not even a NULL key on the other side. To keep such rows, use an outer join from the orders side.

Which queries return Cy with NULL in the order columns? (Choose three.)

options.text: `customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: Customers is the preserved (left) side, so Cy is kept and NULL-padded.

options.text: `orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: Customers is the preserved (right) side, which is the same as the LEFT JOIN above.

options.text: `customers c FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: A FULL JOIN preserves both sides, so Cy appears NULL-padded (and so does order 13).

options.text: `customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: An inner join drops Cy because no order matches.

options.text: `customers c CROSS JOIN orders o`
options.why: Cy appears four times, each time paired with a real order, never with NULLs.

explanation: A row from a table appears NULL-padded only when that table is on the preserved side of an outer join: the left of LEFT, the right of RIGHT, or either side of FULL. A CROSS JOIN pairs Cy with every order, so there are no NULLs.

options.why: Query 1 filters after the join, and Cy's NULL amount fails `> 60`, so Cy is removed.

options.text: Query 1: 2 rows, Query 2: 3 rows
options.why: WHERE removes NULL-padded rows; a condition in ON only limits which orders match.

options.text: Query 1: 2 rows, Query 2: 2 rows
options.why: Query 2 still keeps Cy: an unmet ON condition just means Cy gets NULLs.

options.text: Query 1: 2 rows, Query 2: 4 rows
options.why: Ann's 50 order fails the ON condition, so Ann gets only the 100 row, not an extra NULL row.

explanation: Query 1 runs the LEFT JOIN (4 rows), then WHERE keeps rows with amount > 60: Ann 100 and Bob 70. Cy's NULL amount makes `NULL > 60` unknown, so the LEFT JOIN effectively becomes an INNER JOIN. Query 2 only matches orders above 60, but still keeps every customer: Ann 100, Bob 70, Cy NULL. Put right-table filters in ON when you want to keep unmatched left rows.

Which query returns exactly the customers who have no orders?

options.text: `... FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL`
options.why: An inner join has no NULL-padded rows, so this returns nothing.

options.text: `... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL`
options.why: Only unmatched customers have a NULL in the non-nullable o.id; this returns Cy.

options.text: `... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.id IS NULL`
options.why: c.id comes from the preserved side and is never NULL, so this returns nothing.

options.text: `... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.id IS NULL` (no WHERE)
options.why: In ON, the extra condition just prevents any match, so all three customers come back.

explanation: The LEFT JOIN … IS NULL anti-join keeps customers whose join produced NULL padding. Test a column that can only be NULL because of the padding, such as the right table's primary key. Run on the sample data, the correct query returns only Cy; the ON variant returns Ann, Bob and Cy.

Which queries list each customer who has at least one order exactly once? (Choose three.)

options.text: `SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`
options.why: EXISTS is a semi-join: each customer is returned once however many orders match.

options.text: `SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`
options.why: IN is also a semi-join; the NULL in the subquery doesn't hurt a positive IN test.

options.text: `SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: The join repeats Ann, but DISTINCT on the customer key collapses the duplicates.

options.text: `SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: Ann has two orders, so the plain join returns her twice.

options.text: `SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: The LEFT JOIN also returns Cy, who has no orders, and repeats Ann.

explanation: Joining to test existence multiplies rows by the number of matches. EXISTS and IN express "has at least one", and DISTINCT on the key removes the duplicates a join creates. Results: EXISTS and IN return Ann, Bob; the plain join returns Ann, Ann, Bob.

`posts` has ids 1 and 2. `post_tags` has (1,'a'), (1,'b'), (2,'a'). `comments` has three comments on post 1 and one on post 2. How many rows does this return?

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM posts p
JOIN post_tags t ON t.post_id = p.id
JOIN comments c ON c.post_id = p.id;
```

options.why: That counts comments only; each comment row is repeated once per tag of the same post.
That adds tags and comments; independent one-to-many joins multiply rather than add.
Post 1 gives 2 tags × 3 comments = 6 and post 2 gives 1 × 1 = 1.
That multiplies all tags by all comments; the join keys keep each post's rows separate.

explanation: Joining one parent to two independent child tables creates a Cartesian product per parent: tags × comments. Post 1 contributes 2 × 3 = 6 rows and post 2 contributes 1 × 1 = 1, so 7. This "fan-out" is why counts and sums go wrong after joins; aggregate each child table separately first.

stem: Table `ta(k)` holds 1, 1, 2 and table `tb(k)` holds 1, 1, 1, 3. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM ta JOIN tb ON ta.k = tb.k;` return? Type a number.
explanation: Each of the two 1s in ta matches each of the three 1s in tb: 2 × 3 = 6. The 2 and the 3 have no partners. Duplicate keys on both sides multiply, which is why joining on a non-unique column can silently inflate results.

Forgetting the join predicate in old-style comma joins is a classic source of exploding row counts; explicit `JOIN … ON` makes the omission obvious.

stem: Given `t1(id, a)` and `t2(id, a, b)`, match each query with the number of columns `SELECT *` returns.

options.text: 3 columns
4 columns
5 columns
2 columns

prompts.text: `SELECT * FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON t1.id = t2.id`

explanation: USING (id) merges the listed column into one output column: id, t1.a, t2.a, b (4). NATURAL JOIN uses every same-named column, here id and a, so it outputs id, a, b (3). ON merges nothing: id, a, id, a, b (5). Checked on PostgreSQL 18.

stem: A report uses `SELECT ... FROM orders NATURAL JOIN customers`. If a later migration adds an `updated_at` column to both tables, the report keeps returning the same rows.

options.text: True
options.why: NATURAL JOIN re-reads the column names each time, so the new shared column joins too.

options.text: False
options.why: The join silently becomes `USING (…, updated_at)`, and rows whose timestamps differ stop matching.

explanation: NATURAL JOIN joins on every column name the two tables share. Adding a shared column changes the join condition without touching the query, and usually returns far fewer rows. Spell out the condition with ON or USING so schema changes can't change your joins.

stem: Put these steps in the logical order SQL evaluates a query (ignoring grouping).

options.text: FROM and JOIN … ON: build the joined rows
WHERE: filter the joined rows
SELECT: compute the output columns
ORDER BY: sort the result
LIMIT: keep the first n rows

explanation: Joins (with their ON conditions) are evaluated first, then WHERE filters the joined result, then SELECT computes expressions, then ORDER BY sorts and LIMIT trims. That is why a condition in ON and the same condition in WHERE behave differently for outer joins, and why WHERE can't see SELECT aliases. The planner may physically reorder work, but results must match this logical order.

stem: A `players(id, name)` table has 4 rows. You want every pair of different players exactly once (a-b, but not also b-a). Which self join does that, and how many rows does it return?

options.text: `ON a.id <> b.id`, returning 6 rows
options.why: This returns both orderings of each pair: 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

options.text: `ON a.id < b.id`, returning 6 rows
options.why: Requiring the first id to be smaller keeps one ordering of each pair: 4 × 3 / 2.

options.text: `ON a.id <> b.id` with SELECT DISTINCT, returning 6 rows
options.why: DISTINCT doesn't help: (a, b) and (b, a) are different rows, so 12 remain.

options.text: `CROSS JOIN` with no condition, returning 12 rows
options.why: A cross join returns 16 rows, including each player paired with themself.

explanation: `a.id <> b.id` removes self-pairs but keeps mirrored ones (12 rows). `a.id < b.id` keeps just one orientation of each pair: C(4, 2) = 6. Both counts were checked on PostgreSQL 18.

stem:
`budget(dept, amt)` has ('A',10), ('B',20). `actual(dept, amt)` has ('B',15), ('C',5).

```sql
SELECT b.dept, b.amt AS budget, a.amt AS actual
FROM budget b FULL JOIN actual a ON a.dept = b.dept;
```

The row for department C shows a NULL dept. What is the fix?

options.text: Select `COALESCE(b.dept, a.dept)` as the department
options.why: In a FULL JOIN either side can be NULL, so take the key from whichever side exists.

options.text: Change it to `budget b LEFT JOIN actual a` so every row has a budget dept
options.why: That removes department C entirely, since it has no budget row.

options.text: Add `WHERE b.dept IS NOT NULL` to drop the row
options.why: That hides department C instead of naming it; C still had real spending.

options.text: Join `ON a.dept = b.dept OR b.dept IS NULL`
options.why: That pairs C with nothing useful and adds bogus matches against NULL rows.

explanation: The FULL JOIN returns A (budget only), B (both) and C (actual only). For C, every `b.*` column is NULL, including `b.dept`. Selecting `COALESCE(b.dept, a.dept)` gives A, B, C. `JOIN … USING (dept)` does the same automatically, because its merged column is the COALESCE of both sides.

options.why: trim() does fix the trailing-space row, so Q2 already matches two rows; only the case difference still blocks it.
Plain equality is exact for varchar, trim() recovers the padded row, and lower() on both sides also catches the case variant.
Trailing spaces are ignored only for char(n); varchar comparison is exact, so Q1 matches just one row.
Text equality in PostgreSQL is neither case-insensitive nor space-insensitive under a deterministic collation.

explanation: Join conditions compare keys exactly. With `varchar`, `'AB12 '` differs from `'AB12'` and `'ab12'` differs by case, so Q1 matches 1 row. `trim()` removes the trailing space (2 rows), and `lower(trim(...))` on both sides also folds case (3 rows). If both columns were `char(5)`, trailing spaces would be insignificant and Q1 would already return 2. Normalising inside the ON clause works but defeats a plain index on `code`; the durable fix is to clean keys on load, or add an expression index on `lower(trim(code))`. Verified on PostgreSQL 18.
reference: PostgreSQL docs: Character Types; String Functions

Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

Which queries correctly return the id of every customer with no orders? (Choose three.)

options.text: `SELECT c.id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`
options.why: NOT EXISTS is a true anti-join and ignores the NULL customer_id; it returns 3.

options.text: `SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL`
options.why: Testing the right table's primary key finds the NULL-padded rows; it returns 3.

options.text: `SELECT id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders`
options.why: Set difference {1,2,3} minus {1,2,NULL} is {3}; EXCEPT treats NULLs as equal and has no NOT IN trap.

options.text: `SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`
options.why: The NULL customer_id makes every NOT IN test unknown, so it returns no rows.

options.text: `SELECT c.id FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL`
options.why: An inner join produces no NULL padding, so this returns no rows.

explanation: NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN … IS NULL on a non-nullable column, and EXCEPT all express an anti-join correctly. NOT IN fails as soon as the subquery yields a NULL. On the sample data, A, B and C return 3; D and E return nothing.

stem:
`orders(id, total)` has (1, 100) and (2, 100). `items(order_id, sku)` has two items for order 1 and one for order 2.

```sql
SELECT SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id;
```

It returns 300, but revenue is 200. Why?

options.text: SUM counts NULL totals as zero, which skews the result
options.why: There are no NULL totals here; the problem is duplicated rows, not NULLs.

options.text: Order 1 has two items, so its total appears in two joined rows
options.why: A one-to-many join repeats parent values once per child: 100 + 100 + 100.

options.text: The inner join adds an extra NULL-padded row for order 2
options.why: Inner joins never add NULL-padded rows; order 2 appears once.

options.text: Each order row is doubled by the inner join, regardless of how many items it has
options.why: Only order 1 repeats, because only it has two items; order 2 appears once.

explanation: The join produces one row per item, and each carries its order's total: order 1 contributes 100 twice. This fan-out inflates SUM and COUNT. Aggregate the child table first, or filter with EXISTS instead of joining when you only need parent values.

stem:
Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

`items(order_id, product_id)` has (10,'p1') and (12,'p2'); `products` has 'p1' and 'p2'. How many rows does this return?

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id, p.title
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o   ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN items i    ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p      ON p.id = i.product_id;
```

options.text: 2 rows: the final inner join drops rows with a NULL product_id
options.why: Cy and Ann's order 11 have NULL product_id after the left joins, so the inner join removes them.

options.text: 3 rows: the earlier LEFT JOINs guarantee that Cy is kept
options.why: Joins are applied left to right; a later inner join can still remove NULL-padded rows.

options.text: 4 rows: Ann's order 11 is kept, with a NULL in the product title column
options.why: Order 11 has no item, so its product_id is NULL and fails the inner join.

options.text: 2 rows, because LEFT JOIN items drops orders without items
options.why: LEFT JOIN items keeps order 11; it is the final inner join that removes it.

explanation: The two LEFT JOINs give Ann-10-p1, Ann-11-NULL, Bob-12-p2 and Cy-NULL-NULL. The final INNER JOIN needs `p.id = i.product_id` to be true, which fails for NULL product_id. Only Ann-10-Pen and Bob-12-Pad survive. Mixing an inner join after outer joins quietly undoes them.

stem:
`emp` has salaries 5,000, 10,000 and 60,000. `brackets(low, high, rate)` has (0, 10000, 0.1), (10000, 50000, 0.2) and (50000, 1000000, 0.3).

```sql
SELECT e.name, b.rate
FROM emp e
JOIN brackets b ON e.salary BETWEEN b.low AND b.high;
```

How many rows come back?

options.text: 3, one bracket per employee
options.why: That would need half-open ranges; BETWEEN includes both ends.

options.text: 4, because 10,000 matches two brackets
options.why: BETWEEN is inclusive, so 10,000 equals the high of one bracket and the low of the next.

options.text: 2, because 10,000 falls between brackets
options.why: Inclusive bounds mean 10,000 belongs to both brackets, not neither.

options.text: 9, because a range join compares every pair
options.why: Every pair is compared, but only pairs where the salary lies in the range are kept.

explanation: Range (non-equi) joins need non-overlapping bands. With BETWEEN, a value on a shared boundary falls into two bands and is duplicated. Use half-open intervals, `e.salary >= b.low AND e.salary < b.high`, which returns 3 rows. PostgreSQL range types such as `int4range` with `@>` encode the same rule.
reference: PostgreSQL docs: Comparison Functions and Operators (BETWEEN)

stem:
Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

You need each customer's two largest orders, and customers with no orders must still appear once with NULLs. Each option joins `customers c` to the same subquery, written `(…)` below:

```sql
(SELECT amount FROM orders o
 WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
 ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 2) t
```

Which join form keeps Cy?

options.text: `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (…) t`
options.why: CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops a customer whose subquery returns no rows, so Cy disappears.

options.text: `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) t ON true`
options.why: LEFT JOIN LATERAL keeps customers whose subquery is empty, padding with NULLs.

options.text: `JOIN LATERAL (…) t ON t.amount IS NOT NULL`
options.why: An inner LATERAL join also drops customers whose subquery returns no rows.

options.text: `, LATERAL (…) t` (comma syntax)
options.why: A comma before LATERAL is a cross join, so Cy is dropped just as with CROSS JOIN LATERAL.

explanation: A LATERAL subquery runs once per outer row and can reference it, which makes it the natural tool for top-N per group. With CROSS JOIN, an inner JOIN or a comma, an empty subquery removes the outer row. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps it: Ann 100, Ann 50, Bob 70, Cy NULL (checked on PostgreSQL 18).

stem: Match each situation with the join algorithm the PostgreSQL planner typically chooses.

options.text: Nested loop
Hash join
Merge join

prompts.text: A join whose only condition is a range, such as `b.id BETWEEN s.lo AND s.hi`
Two large, unsorted inputs joined on an equality condition
Both inputs can be read already sorted on the equality join key, for example through indexes

explanation: Hash and merge joins both need an equality condition: a hash join builds a hash table on one input and probes it, and a merge join walks two sorted inputs in step. For range-only conditions only a nested loop works, ideally probing an index on the inner side. On PostgreSQL 18, a big/small equality join produced a Hash Join and a BETWEEN join produced a Nested Loop with an index scan.

stem: PostgreSQL can execute a join whose only condition is `b.id BETWEEN s.id AND s.id + 5` as a hash join.

options.text: True
options.why: A hash join can only look up equal keys; it can't find all keys inside a range.

options.text: False
options.why: Range conditions have no equality to hash on, so the planner falls back to a nested loop.

explanation: Hash joins (and merge joins) require at least one equality clause between the inputs. For this query, PostgreSQL 18 chose a Nested Loop that probes the index on `big.id` with `Index Cond: ((id >= s.id) AND (id <= (s.id + 5)))`. For big range joins, make sure the inner side has a usable index.

stem: `child.parent_id` has a `REFERENCES parent(id)` constraint, and `parent.id` is its primary key. Which statements about indexes are true in PostgreSQL? (Choose two.)

options.text: The primary key on `parent.id` is backed by an automatically created unique index
options.why: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints always create an index to enforce uniqueness.

options.text: No index is created on `child.parent_id`; you must add one yourself if you need it
options.why: PostgreSQL never auto-indexes the referencing column; only child_pkey existed in the test.

options.text: Declaring the foreign key makes joins on `parent_id` use an index automatically
options.why: A constraint isn't an index; without one, joins and lookups on parent_id scan child.

options.text: An index on `child.parent_id` must exist before the constraint can be declared
options.why: The referenced side needs a unique index; the referencing side needs none.

options.text: Foreign key checks run only once, when the transaction commits
options.why: They run per statement by default; only DEFERRABLE constraints can wait until commit.

explanation: PostgreSQL requires a unique index on the referenced columns and creates one for a primary key. It doesn't index the referencing column. Without that index, deleting or updating a parent row has to scan the whole child table to check for references, and joins from parent to child can't use an index. Indexing foreign key columns is a routine performance step.

stem: `fa(k)` holds 1, 2, 2, NULL and `fb(k)` holds 2, 3, NULL. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM fa FULL JOIN fb ON fa.k = fb.k;` return? Type a number.
explanation: The two 2s in fa each match the 2 in fb: 2 rows. Then the unmatched rows from fa (1 and NULL) and from fb (3 and NULL) are added, NULL-padded: 4 rows. NULLs never match each other with `=`. Total 6, checked on PostgreSQL 18.

```sql
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')

(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

`items(order_id, product_id)` has (10,'p1') and (12,'p2'). You want every customer, each with only those orders that have a product, and customers without such orders shown once with NULLs. Which FROM clause gives Ann-10, Bob-12 and Cy-NULL?

options.text: `c LEFT JOIN orders o ON … LEFT JOIN items i ON … LEFT JOIN products p ON …`
options.why: Making every join LEFT also keeps Ann's order 11 with a NULL product: 4 rows.

options.text: `c LEFT JOIN (orders o JOIN items i ON … JOIN products p ON …) ON o.customer_id = c.id`
options.why: The parentheses inner-join orders to products first, then left-join that result to customers.

options.text: `c LEFT JOIN orders o ON … LEFT JOIN items i ON … LEFT JOIN products p ON … WHERE p.id IS NOT NULL`
options.why: The WHERE filter removes Cy's NULL row as well, giving 2 rows.

options.text: `products p LEFT JOIN items i ON … LEFT JOIN orders o ON … LEFT JOIN customers c ON …`
options.why: Starting from products preserves products, not customers, so Cy never appears.

explanation: Join order matters with outer joins. Parenthesising `orders JOIN items JOIN products` makes it one unit (only orders with a product), which the LEFT JOIN then attaches to customers. Customers with no such order are NULL-padded once. PostgreSQL 18 returned exactly Ann-10-Pen, Bob-12-Pad, Cy-NULL.

stem: `budget(dept, amt)` and `actual(dept, amt)` are joined with `budget FULL JOIN actual USING (dept)`. Which statements are true in PostgreSQL? (Choose three.)

options.text: `SELECT *` shows the `dept` column once, not twice
options.why: USING merges the listed columns into a single output column.

options.text: An unqualified `dept` in the SELECT list is allowed and unambiguous
options.why: The merged column can be referenced without a table name.

options.text: For the FULL JOIN, the merged `dept` equals `COALESCE(budget.dept, actual.dept)`
options.why: Rows from either side show their department, unlike a qualified column.

options.text: Qualified references such as `budget.dept` are rejected after USING
options.why: They are allowed; `budget.dept` is just NULL for rows that exist only in actual.

options.text: USING requires both columns to have exactly the same data type
options.why: Compatible types such as int and bigint can be joined with USING.

explanation: With USING, the output column is effectively `COALESCE(left.col, right.col)` for outer joins, appears once in `SELECT *`, and can be used unqualified. The original columns are still reachable through their table names. All of this was confirmed on PostgreSQL 18, including an int-to-bigint USING join.

stem:
`small.id` is a primary key. EXPLAIN for this query shows only `Seq Scan on big b`, with no join at all:

```sql
SELECT b.id
FROM big b
LEFT JOIN small s ON s.id = b.small_id;
```

Why can PostgreSQL skip the join?

options.text: `small` is tiny, so the planner caches it in memory instead of performing the join
options.why: Size isn't the reason; the join would still be planned if it could change the result.

options.text: No `small` column is used, and a unique key means at most one match per row
options.why: A LEFT JOIN to a unique key can neither remove nor duplicate rows of big, so it is dead weight.

options.text: LEFT JOINs are never executed when the query has no WHERE clause
options.why: They are executed whenever they can affect the output; this one can't.

options.text: A foreign key guarantees every small_id has a matching row
options.why: No foreign key is declared here, and with an inner join PostgreSQL still kept the join.

explanation: This is join removal. A LEFT JOIN never drops left rows, and joining on a unique column can't duplicate them, so if no right-hand column is referenced the join can be removed. The same query as an INNER JOIN still showed a Hash Join on PostgreSQL 18, because an inner join could drop rows with no match.

Order these queries by the number of rows they return, fewest first.

options.text: `customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
`customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
`customers c FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`
`customers c CROSS JOIN orders o`

explanation: INNER returns the 3 matching pairs. LEFT adds Cy: 4. FULL also adds order 13, whose customer is NULL: 5. CROSS returns every combination: 3 × 4 = 12. All four counts were checked on PostgreSQL 18.

stem:
Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

A customer Dee (id 4) is added with one order, (14, 4, NULL), whose amount is unknown. This "customers without orders" query now returns Cy and Dee:

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.amount IS NULL;
```

What is wrong?

options.text: LEFT JOIN treats an order with a NULL amount as if it were a missing match
options.why: Dee's order matched; it's the WHERE test that can't tell real NULLs from padding.

options.text: amount can be NULL in real rows; test a non-nullable column like o.id
options.why: A NULL check on a nullable column can't distinguish real NULLs from LEFT JOIN padding.

options.text: The `o.amount IS NULL` filter must move from WHERE into the ON clause
options.why: In ON, `o.amount IS NULL` would match Dee's order and return every customer.

options.text: Dee needs a NOT NULL constraint on customers.name
options.why: Customer names don't affect which orders match.

explanation: In a LEFT JOIN anti-join, a NULL in the right-hand column must mean "no match". If the column can hold real NULLs, matched rows slip through. Test the right table's primary key (or the join column itself), or use NOT EXISTS. On PostgreSQL 18, `o.amount IS NULL` returned Cy and Dee; `o.id IS NULL` returned only Cy.

Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

A dashboard shows order counts per customer, and Cy shows 1 even though Cy has no orders:

```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
```

What is the fix?

options.text: Switch to an inner join so Cy's row is counted correctly
options.why: That removes Cy altogether instead of showing 0.

options.text: Use `COUNT(o.id)`, which skips the NULL-padded row
options.why: COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, so Cy's padded row counts as 0.

options.text: Use `COUNT(DISTINCT c.name)`, which ignores missing orders
options.why: That counts 1 per customer group, which is 1 for everyone.

options.text: Add `WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL`, which keeps Cy at 0
options.why: That removes Cy's only row, so Cy disappears from the result.

explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, and the LEFT JOIN gives Cy one NULL-padded row. COUNT(o.id) counts non-NULL values only. On PostgreSQL 18: COUNT(*) gives Ann 2, Bob 1, Cy 1; COUNT(o.id) gives Ann 2, Bob 1, Cy 0.

stem: `orders(id, total)` has (1, 100) and (2, 100). `items(order_id, sku)` has two items for order 1 and one for order 2. Joining them makes `SUM(o.total)` return 300 instead of 200. Which rewrites return 200? (Choose two.)

options.text: Join orders to `(SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM items GROUP BY order_id)` and sum the totals
options.why: Pre-aggregating the child table gives one row per order, so nothing repeats.

options.text: `SELECT SUM(total) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT o.id, o.total FROM orders o JOIN items i ON …) s`
options.why: De-duplicating on the order key first restores one row per order.

options.text: Replace `SUM(o.total)` with `SUM(DISTINCT o.total)`
options.why: Both orders total 100, so DISTINCT collapses them and returns 100.

options.text: Change the inner join to a LEFT JOIN
options.why: The fan-out is the same; LEFT JOIN still returns 300.

options.text: Add `GROUP BY o.id` and keep `SUM(o.total)`
options.why: That returns one row per order, and order 1 still shows 200.

explanation: To sum parent values across a one-to-many join, remove the multiplication first: aggregate the child per parent, or reduce to distinct parent keys. SUM(DISTINCT value) de-duplicates values, not rows, so two orders with equal totals merge. PostgreSQL 18 results: A and B give 200, C gives 100, D gives 300, E gives 200 and 100.

stem: `fa(k)` holds 1, 2, 2, NULL and `fb(k)` holds 2, 3, NULL. How many rows do these inner joins return: `ON fa.k = fb.k`, and `ON fa.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM fb.k`?

options.text: 2 and 2, because the second form only differs for outer joins
options.why: It differs for any join: it changes whether NULL matches NULL.

options.text: 2 and 3, because the second form also matches NULL with NULL
options.why: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM treats two NULLs as equal, adding one NULL-NULL pair.

options.text: 3 and 3, because `=` already treats NULLs as equal in joins
options.why: `NULL = NULL` is unknown, so the plain equality join skips it.

options.text: 2 and 4, because the NULL matches every row on the other side
options.why: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM matches NULL only to NULL, not to every value.

explanation: With `=`, the two 2s in fa each match the 2 in fb: 2 rows. `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` is a NULL-safe comparison, so the two NULLs also match: 3 rows. Use it when NULL means "same unknown bucket" (rare in keys). Note that it can prevent index use for the NULL case.
reference: PostgreSQL docs: Comparison Predicates (IS DISTINCT FROM)

stem: PostgreSQL chose a Hash Join for `big JOIN small ON small.id = big.small_id`, and EXPLAIN shows `small` under the Hash node. Put the steps of the hash join in order.

options.text: Scan small and build an in-memory hash table keyed on small.id
Start reading big row by row
Hash each big row's small_id and look up the matching bucket
Recheck the join condition for bucket entries and emit each matching pair

explanation: A hash join first builds a hash table from one input, normally the smaller one (the child of the Hash node in EXPLAIN). It then streams the other input, hashing each join key to probe the table and rechecking the actual condition, since different keys can share a bucket. If the hash table exceeds work_mem it is split into batches on disk.

`docs(id, tags text[])` has (1, '{x,y}'), (2, '{}') and (3, NULL). How many rows do these return?

```sql
-- Query 1
SELECT d.id, t FROM docs d, unnest(d.tags) t;

-- Query 2
SELECT d.id, t FROM docs d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL unnest(d.tags) t ON true;
```

options.text: 4 and 4
options.why: In Query 1, an empty or NULL array produces no rows, so docs 2 and 3 vanish.

options.text: 3 and 4
options.why: unnest of a NULL array returns no rows, not one NULL element.

options.text: 2 and 4
options.why: The comma (cross) join drops docs with no elements; LEFT JOIN LATERAL keeps them as NULL.

options.text: 2 and 3
options.why: Both doc 2 (empty) and doc 3 (NULL) are kept by the LEFT JOIN, giving 4.

explanation: A set-returning function in FROM is an implicit LATERAL cross join: a row whose function returns zero rows disappears. Doc 1 yields x and y; docs 2 and 3 yield nothing. LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true keeps them with t = NULL. PostgreSQL 18 returned 2 and 4 rows.

stem:
For `SELECT * FROM small s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM big b WHERE b.small_id = s.id)`, PostgreSQL 18 produced:

```text
Hash Join
  Hash Cond: (s.id = b.small_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on small s
  ->  Hash
        ->  HashAggregate
              Group Key: b.small_id
              ->  Seq Scan on big b
```

big has 2,000 rows per small_id. Why doesn't each small row come back 2,000 times?

options.text: A Hash Join always discards duplicate matches for a key
options.why: An ordinary hash join emits every matching pair; it does not de-duplicate.

options.text: The HashAggregate reduces big to distinct small_id values before the join
options.why: Joining against unique keys is equivalent to the semi-join that EXISTS asks for.

options.text: small.id is a primary key, so the join can't produce any duplicate small rows
options.why: Duplicates would come from the big side, where small_id repeats.

options.text: EXISTS is always rewritten as IN with DISTINCT on the outer table
options.why: The plan de-duplicates the inner (big) side, not small.

explanation: EXISTS is a semi-join: return each outer row at most once. The planner can run it as a Semi Join node, or, as here, make the inner side unique (HashAggregate on b.small_id) and then do a regular join. Both give one row per matching small row. Joining without DISTINCT would return 2,000 copies.

stem:
`staff(id, name, manager_id)` holds (1,'Ceo',NULL), (2,'Vp',1), (3,'Dev',2). How many rows does this return?

```sql
SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager, mm.name AS skip_level
FROM staff e
LEFT JOIN staff m  ON m.id  = e.manager_id
JOIN staff mm      ON mm.id = m.manager_id;
```

options.text: 1: only Dev, whose manager also has a manager
options.why: The inner join needs m.manager_id to match; it is NULL for Ceo (no m) and for Vp (m is Ceo).

options.text: 3: the LEFT JOIN keeps every employee
options.why: The later inner join removes rows whose m.manager_id has no match.

options.text: 2: Vp and Dev, because both have a manager
options.why: Vp's manager (Ceo) has no manager, so the second join removes Vp.

options.text: 0: Ceo has no manager, so the inner join fails for everyone
options.why: Each row is checked on its own; Dev still finds Vp, then Ceo.

explanation: The LEFT JOIN gives (Ceo, NULL), (Vp, Ceo) and (Dev, Vp). The INNER JOIN then requires a skip-level manager: Ceo's row has no m, and Ceo has no manager, so only Dev → Vp → Ceo survives. Make the second join LEFT too to keep all three. Recursive CTEs handle hierarchies of any depth.

stem: A query has `FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id`. Which additions turn it into an inner join in effect, removing the `a` rows that have no `b`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `WHERE b.status = 'active'`
options.why: For unmatched rows b.status is NULL, so the comparison is unknown and the row is dropped.

options.text: `WHERE b.created_at IS NOT NULL`
options.why: b.created_at is NULL in every padded row, so they are all removed.

options.text: `JOIN c ON c.id = b.c_id` after the LEFT JOIN
options.why: The inner join needs b.c_id to match, which fails for padded rows.

options.text: Adding `AND b.status = 'active'` to the ON clause
options.why: Conditions in ON only limit matches; unmatched a rows are still kept.

options.text: `WHERE COALESCE(b.qty, 0) >= 0`
options.why: The COALESCE turns NULL into 0, so padded rows pass and are kept.

explanation: Any condition that is false or unknown for NULL-padded b rows, applied after the join, discards them, and so does a later inner join on a b column. That is the most common way LEFT JOINs silently become inner joins. To filter b but keep all a rows, put the condition in ON, or use a NULL-tolerant predicate.

stem:
For an anti-join on `small` and `big` (where `big.small_id` is nullable), PostgreSQL 18 plans the two forms differently:

```text
-- NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM big b WHERE b.small_id = s.id)
Nested Loop Anti Join

-- s.id NOT IN (SELECT small_id FROM big)
Seq Scan on small s
  Filter: (NOT (ANY (id = (hashed SubPlan 1).col1)))
```

Why can't the planner turn NOT IN into an Anti Join?

options.text: NOT IN subqueries are always executed once per outer row, which rules out a join plan
options.why: Here the subplan is hashed and run once; the issue is semantics, not repetition.

options.text: A NULL from the subquery makes NOT IN unknown, which an anti-join can't express
options.why: An anti-join would return unmatched rows even when a NULL is present, changing the result.

options.text: Anti joins require an index on the inner side, and big.small_id doesn't have one
options.why: The NOT EXISTS form got an anti join with no index at all.

options.text: NOT IN compares with <> while anti-joins can only use =
options.why: Both are equality-based; the NULL rule is what blocks the rewrite.

explanation: NOT EXISTS returns outer rows that have no matching inner row, which is exactly an anti-join. NOT IN must return no rows at all if the subquery contains a NULL, so it can only become an anti-join when both sides are provably non-NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS: it is correct with NULLs and gives the planner more options.

stem:
`budget(dept, amt)` has ('A',10), ('B',20); `actual(dept, amt)` has ('B',15), ('C',5). Which departments does this return?

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(b.dept, a.dept) AS dept
FROM budget b FULL JOIN actual a ON a.dept = b.dept
WHERE b.amt > 0;
```

options.text: A, B and C
options.why: For C, b.amt is NULL, so `b.amt > 0` is unknown and the row is removed.

options.text: A and B
options.why: The WHERE test on a budget column drops rows that exist only in actual.

options.text: B only
options.why: A has a budget of 10, so it passes the filter even without an actual row.

options.text: A, B and C, with a NULL budget for C
options.why: The filter runs after the join and rejects C's NULL-padded budget.

explanation: A WHERE condition on one side of a FULL JOIN discards rows padded on that side, so this FULL JOIN behaves like `budget LEFT JOIN actual`. PostgreSQL 18 returned A and B. To keep C, write `WHERE b.amt > 0 OR b.dept IS NULL`, or move the filter into a subquery on budget.

stem:
Tables:

```sql
-- customers(id, name)
(1, 'Ann'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Cy')
-- orders(id, customer_id, amount)
(10, 1, 100), (11, 1, 50), (12, 2, 70), (13, NULL, 30)
```

How many rows does this return?

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND c.name = 'Ann';
```

options.text: 2: only Ann's orders, because the ON clause filters customers
options.why: An ON condition can't remove rows from the preserved (left) table.

options.text: 4: Ann twice, plus Bob and Cy with NULL order ids
options.why: Bob and Cy fail the ON condition, so they get NULL padding rather than being dropped.

options.text: 3: Ann twice and Bob once, since Bob does have an order
options.why: Bob's order can't match while c.name = 'Ann' is false for Bob, so Bob is NULL-padded.

options.text: 5: every customer plus order 13, which has no customer
options.why: This is a LEFT JOIN from customers, so unmatched orders are never added.

explanation: In a LEFT JOIN, the ON clause decides only which right rows match; every left row survives. A condition on the left table in ON therefore stops Bob's order from matching but keeps Bob, padded with NULLs. PostgreSQL 18 returned (Ann, 10), (Ann, 11), (Bob, NULL), (Cy, NULL). Put filters on the preserved table in WHERE.
